results.summary: This Wokwi project is intended to implement eight-input logic gates using all eight inputs of the tile. The documentation states the gates are planned but not yet built, so the design is essentially a hello-world placeholder. Testing would involve setting the eight input pins and observing the corresponding outputs. No external hardware is required, and the project is notable only as an introductory template.

This design demonstrates trivial AND gates and inverters on a Tiny Tapeout tile, with OUT0 combining IN0 and a reset signal, OUT1 combining IN0 and IN1, OUT2 and OUT3 inverting IN2 and IN3, and OUT4 through OUT7 passing inputs straight through. It is meant to illustrate logical inputs and outputs, the tool flow, and 3D visualization. Testing uses a reset pushbutton, DIP switches for inputs, and an LED display for outputs. The project is a simple educational gate sample rather than a functional application.

This project is described as an introduction to Tiny Tapeout built around AND gates that do not do much. The author states they are still figuring out how it works, and the pin list is inconsistent, with uo[3] labelled OUT4. Testing is said to involve flipping DIP switches, and a 7-segment display is listed as external hardware. The documentation is too thin to determine the actual logic function.

This design proposes a pseudo random generator built from two ring oscillators whose outputs are sampled by a D flip-flop at a 10 kHz clock. OUT0 and OUT1 are described as complementary random outputs. The documentation says only that power should be connected and that the oscillators will in theory start oscillating. No external hardware is required, but the design is speculative and no silicon results are reported.

This project is titled Drew's First Wokwi Design and its documentation says only that it is a thing that does stuff. Testing is described as hooking it up to things and seeing if it does stuff, and the external hardware is called a mystery. The pin list includes eight inputs, eight bidirectional pins and eight outputs, but no function is specified. The documentation is essentially unusable for determining what the design does.

This design places four NAND gates on a tile, with each gate taking two input pins and driving one output pin. The description says it is a bunch of NANDs intended to test the tool chain for now. Testing is described informally as manually connecting the NAND inputs. No external hardware is specified, and the project is a simple tool-chain exercise rather than a useful circuit.

This project drives a seven-segment display to spell the letters J, O and N depending on which of three input pins is asserted. Pin 1 outputs J, pin 2 outputs O and pin 3 outputs N according to the documentation. A seven-segment display is the only external hardware required. The design is a beginner exercise with minimal documentation and no reported silicon results.

This design steps through the five letters of the name AAron on a seven-segment display each time a clock button is pressed. The documentation notes that the letters for 0 and 1 are the same, so the sequence has a quirk. A seven-segment display is the only external hardware needed. It is a simple educational character-sequencing project with no reported silicon results.

This project implements a simple set-reset latch using two input pins and two output pins. IN1 acts as the set input, driving OUT0 high and OUT1 low, while IN0 acts as the reset input, driving OUT0 low and OUT1 high. No external hardware is required. The documentation is minimal and does not describe behaviour when both inputs are asserted or released.

This design is a six-bit shift register that takes a clock and serial data input and presents the six stored bits on output pins 0 through 5. Testing is done by applying a clock and data on inputs 0 and 1 and observing the outputs. Most other pins are marked as not connected, and no external hardware is required. The documentation is very brief and gives no timing or reset details.
